newsitem.title: FRANCE: RENAULT'S TECHNOCRAT CHIEF SCHWEITZER HITS TROUBLE.
newsitem.headline: RENAULT'S TECHNOCRAT CHIEF SCHWEITZER HITS TROUBLE.

text.p: Renault SA chairman Louis Schweitzer, a technocrat turned captain of industry, faces the most serious crisis of his career over his plan to slim down the ailing French carmaker by axing jobs in France and Belgium.

The Belgian government, trade unions and media have accused him of arrogance, heartlessness and a lack of consultation after Renault announced last week it was closing its car plant at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, with the loss of 3,100 jobs.

French trade unions said the company, which expects to announce a substantial loss later this month, notified them on Tuesday that it would also shed 2,764 jobs in France this year and transfer another 1,032 positions within the group.

A senior French parliamentarian, Gaullist floor leader Michel Pericard, criticised Schweitzer over the Belgian decision, saying: "There is no reason why things should be so sudden and brutal without anyone being consulted or prepared."
Unions have called for a one-hour protest strike at Renault plants across Europe on Friday and one union leader on Tuesday forecast a long labour conflict.
A great nephew of Nobel prize winner Albert Schweitzer, Louis Schweitzer has embodied the handover of French state firms to private hands while retaining their civil servant managers.

Schweitzer, a product of France's elite Ecole Nationale d'Administration civil service college, served as chief aide to Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius in 1984-86. A Socialist cabinet made him chairman of the then state-owned firm in 1992.

He presided first over the sale of a minority stake to the public in 1994 and then, last year, over the end of the state's majority shareholding in the company nationalised by General Charles de Gaulle in 1946.

Even though Schweitzer is under judicial investigation in two cases dating back to his government service -- one involving AIDS-tainted blood transfusions and the other illegal bugging by aides of the late president Francois Mitterrand -- the conservative government confirmed him in office in June 1996.

At Renault, he has shown he is more than just a painfully shy technocrat. Regarded as intelligent and hard-working, this modern art lover and avant-garde theatre fan had a reputation for being honest, austere and secretive.
But relatives say the enterprise culture has made him more assertive. "He doesn't stare at his shoes any more and stands straighter when he speaks," one told financial daily Les Echos.

Schweitzer has overseen the carmaker's difficult transition from a cosseted state company with more than 150,000 workers to private manufacturer struggling to succeed despite slow growth in car sales in Europe and fierce competition from its rivals.
But company officials said Renault had deferred long overdue rationalisation measures due to the slow privatisation process and now had to slim down fast to stay competitive.
The smallest of Europe's Big Six carmakers, Renault entered the private sector only in 1996 when the government reduced its stake to 46 percent.
Former chairman Georges Besse invited Schweitzer to join Renault as finance director after the Socialists lost power in 1986, a few months before leftist urban guerrillas killed Besse.
Besse's successor, Raymond Levy, anointed the austere Protestant, better with figures than with people, as his heir.

"He is more rational and less charismatic (than his predecessors), but his answers to questions are very clear and he sticks to them, which is a rather pleasant change," a senior Renault manager told French magazine Le Nouvel Economiste.
Though his first passion was trains, he developed a strong interest in cars and became knowledgeable about engineering, winning the trust of technicians at the company.

Critics say Schweitzer is reluctant to delegate and decides alone. His scepticism about the whimsical Twingo mini-car when he was finance director raised doubts about his willingness to innovate, but he has since shown an eye for new ideas.

Born in 1942 in Geneva to a French protestant family which boasted the theologian and missionary Albert Schweitzer as well as philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre and conductor Charles Munch, he is married with two daughters.
